doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Holman, Russo and Mulligan arrangements for Konitz
summary: They discuss pieces by Holman and Russo, Mulligan's charts, and Mulligan's 1957 big band date.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let’s go back a bit though. I want to talk about some of the things that Holman and Russo wrote for you. You told me years ago that one of your favorites of those was “In A Lighter Vein”. What were some other things that you were particularly fond of that you were featured on?
Of Holman’s?
And Russo.
He wrote an arrangement of “Lover Man”.
They both did right?
Later. I think Bill wrote his for Bird and I recorded that. A few that he wrote for Bird: “My Funny Valentine” and something else.
“Cherokee”.
Yeah. “Cherokee”.
Lennie Niehaus ended up doing that one. There’s a Holman Chart on “Cherokee” that was done for Bird but then later on the “Contemporary Concepts” album Lennie Niehaus played the solo on that.
Really? I thought I played all those arrangements. Bill wrote an original tune called “My Lady” and another one that was a kind of stretch-out piece, I don’t remember what that was called.
“Introspection”?
No, something else. Then Russo wrote some nice arrangements with about four or five horn voicing themes. Some of his better so-called “jazz” arrangements.
Russo and Holman were kind of Yin and Yang for that band.

Something like that, yeah. I remember I went to a record store in Boston to get that record of Holman tunes and I put it on and it was Russo’s tunes by mistake somehow or other. It was quite a different feeling.
I can imagine. Mulligan wrote a handful of charts like “Young Blood” that you played a solo on.

His charts were always fun to play on the Thornhill band and on that band also. That was his forte ultimately. I don’t know the music he wrote for his own band over the later years. It always sounded nice but I don’t remember if it was particularly nice.
Do you remember the nineteen fifty-seven big band date that you played on with him?
I just heard that again. It was really nice.

One of those charts was originally written for Kenton. I think “All the Things You Are”. He wrote a handful of dance charts for Kenton in addition to “Young Blood”, “Swing House”, “Wee-Bidda-Bo-Bidda”, “Walking Shoes” and a handful of other things intended to be dance charts and then he re-wrote one or two of them for that date that you were on.
That was nice. They did one of his originals; “Millennium” I think it was called. It sounded like a Monk tune a little bit.
It sounds like “I Mean You”. So over all it was a positive experience for you?
